translations.text: March 6. The miracles of Saint Conon of Isauria.
In the days of the holy apostles.
When Paul, the preacher and apostle to the whole world, was proclaiming to people the divinity of the Word and the divine plan of the incarnation, he traveled among the nations.
He also reached the regions of Isauria.
He heard that all their cities and settlements were subject to demons through the deceptions of idols, more than those of other nations.
He wanted to go to the mountainous places, but the Holy Spirit prevented him because of their great unbelief, since they would not accept the preaching.
Following the Lord's saying, “Do not throw your pearls before swine,” he turned away from them.
He compelled himself to preach the word without causing anyone to stumble to others who had already been waiting for it, according to the revelation of the Holy Spirit.
Afterward, there was a certain Nestor in those places.
He proved to be of good stock and had a wife named Nada.
They lived in a village called Vidana, eighteen stadia from the city of Isauria. They brought forth a devout child and named him Conon.
When he reached maturity, his parents agreed to marry him to a maiden named Anna.
When the time for the wedding arrived, the archangel Michael appeared to Conon.

He appeared as a man in shining clothing, and as he spoke with Conon, he instructed him in the true mysteries. Conon was persuaded and immediately devoted his heart to them and asked for baptism. He pleaded with the archangel as with a man, thinking him to be human.
The archangel, seeing that Conon had been persuaded, had accepted the word with his whole mind, and was asking for baptism, led him to the water.
He immersed him in the name of the holy and blessed Trinity, gave him communion, and marked him with the sign.
After sanctifying him, he departed invisibly. For he had remained visibly with him until Conon was sanctified and filled with the Holy Spirit.
His parents, unaware of this, made arrangements for the marriage, brought the bride, and married him. But first he took a burning lamp and placed it under a basket.
He said to his wife, who was still a virgin, “Which is sweeter, light or darkness?”
She answered, “Light is sweeter.” Adding other words of instruction through the grace given him by the Holy Spirit, he changed the maiden's mind.
They remained chaste and labored steadfastly, preserving their bodies undefiled in complete purity.
The righteous man's mother heard, rejoiced, and praised her. And they continued in that way of life.
Afterward, through the grace of the archangel, he also converted his father and made him a good servant of God.
Indeed, his father even suffered martyrdom for Christ.
When Saint Conon's chaste wife died, he laid her in one tomb with his mother. He himself remained alone, growing in all patience and labor.
He kept the treasure of spiritual grace given to him until the time came for it to be revealed. Now, when they were holding a great festival for Apollo,
In a certain fearsome and dark cave.
There, according to their custom, the city of Isaura used to hold an assembly.
Many tens of thousands of men and women from Isauria gathered there. The place lies among ravines and impassable mountains, four stadia from the city. On that day, as the people were gathering,
and were about to leave the city, Saint Conon suddenly approached and appeared to them in that city.
Seeing them armed and prepared for the impious acts that lay ahead, he cried out to them in their own language, saying, “Men, wait, so that I may ask you a question.”
He said to them, “Why have you rushed out as though in battle formation?
Is some urgent war calling you?” They said, “No, but today we are offering a sacrifice to the god Apollo.”
The saint said to them, “I would like to know who this Apollo is. What power does he have?
Or what is his strength?” They said to him, “He guides us and strengthens us in war, just as he did our fathers.
For they handed these customs down to us.” Saint Conon questioned them mockingly: “Have you, then, heard his voice?

Or have you spoken to him?” They said, “No, but the custom of our fathers has convinced us.” He said to them, “But your fathers were deceived like irrational animals, having no knowledge of the true God.
For if they had known him, they would not have devoted so much effort to a deaf and motionless stone.
Give me authority over it, and I will show you whom you honor and who your god is. Let me daub it with ink, so that I may see whether it can wash itself.
And give me an iron hammer, and I will smash it, and we shall see whether it can return to its own shape.
I will offer it food: let it stretch out its hand, take it, and eat. How long will you remain foolish, without understanding this?
But now listen to me, for I too am of your people,
though a stranger to you in my deeds. Turn away from these things, and I will teach you whom you should honor
and worship: God, who sits on high, who is a mighty God, invisible yet seeing all things, the Creator of heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them,
a strong and mighty King, who saves his own in battle,
but destroys his enemies. To those who serve idols and sacrifice to demons rather than to God, he is a fierce enemy.
He does not ask for bloody sacrifices, but wishes to be known without stumbling by those who come to him, without deceit and without malice.
They are to believe in him as the true God and the Father of the only-begotten Son,
who is true God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is inseparable from the Father, and for whose sake he also made the ages. The Holy Spirit shares in his divinity and kingship and in those of his Son.
He proceeds from the Father, doing good, and is above all [?].
These, then, bearing three names, are one Godhead. There is one God.
He is jealous, and a fire consuming his enemies, who honor idols as gods
and sacrifice to demons. He burns among them on the day of wrath and takes vengeance.
But he is exceedingly merciful to all who call upon him and believe in him, especially those who turn to him from ungodliness. He also loves those who love him.
He also glorifies those who glorify him. He rejoices in peace, when people love one another.
He also delights in purity of life and in humility, for he hates evil [?]
and rejoices in what is good. If you do not love him, it is clear that you are evil and rebellious.
and you will not be able to endure his wrath. But listen, and do not harden your necks against him, since, as I said, you will not be able to endure the fury of his wrath.

For he is suddenly angered against such people. And as for the way you are now like senseless men, in the service of the devil who deceives you: leave him, turn away from him, and turn to our Lord Jesus Christ, and he will fill all of you with good things. While he was teaching them these things,
to turn away from such madness and turn to the saving proclamation,
they persisted in disobeying him, even turning against him in anger as he was turning

[?] them from their sacrifices, or rather restraining them by force. An uproar arose among them. Some rushed to kill him, while others stopped them and held them back, because they found some pleasure in listening.

They wanted to turn back, but they were not yet fully resolved. When those who seemed to be turning back had barely quieted the uproar, they began to say to the righteous man, “How can you convince us that there is a God?”

greater than our god, whom we hold in honor?” Although he spoke at length to them and taught them, they would not submit at all, but disbelieved all the more. They went so far as to ask him for miracles, saying to him, “What can the one you worship do, so that we may believe in him?
Show us at least one sign, then, and we will believe in him and in you.”
When Saint Conon saw their unbelief was so great that they even asked for a sign, he said to them, “Give me a little time, and we will do this.
Are there not young men among you with strong legs, others stronger still, and some on horseback?
Let us all go to the place where you assemble. You go ahead, and I, being old, will follow. Let us give one another our word: whoever gets ahead
and reaches that place first—
his God is mighty. But let the god of whoever comes last be punished,
since he is not a god.” Seeing his old age, they mocked him and agreed, trusting in the speed of their horses and in their own legs. For they said to one another, “He will not reach the place
for four days. How will he endure such a long journey,
so arduous and mountainous?” But God’s holy Conon, realizing that they had given him up as unable to complete this challenge, roused himself all the more, and prayed alone, saying:
“Master, Lord God, Father Almighty,

Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake the world came into being, strengthen me and lead this whole multitude astray, so that they may learn how they are deceived about those in whom they believe. Fill them, so that they may understand that you are God and there is no other besides you.
And may the holy archangel Michael receive me, who brought me to the knowledge of you and enabled me to know your mystery from childhood.
And immediately Saint Michael came, strengthened the saint, and brought him to the place without difficulty, while invisibly leading the others astray.
Having set out on their journey, they wandered about and battered themselves against the mountains,
tossing about against the walls all that day and that night, until they had no strength left, nor any sound flesh or bone, and could not move from one place to another.
Saint Conon, however, having gone ahead, rose early the next day and turned back. He found them in the very place where he had left them.
When they suddenly saw him, they were terrified. He approached them and confronted them, taking hold of them and saying, “What have you done?
You have left me waiting until now, while I have been expecting you. Growing weary of waiting, I turned back to you.”
Exhausted and breathless, they told him what had happened and begged him to guide them onto the road.
He agreed and offered a prayer, removing from them the blindness brought upon them by the archangel. Then everyone who was there followed him.
When they reached the place, the saint said to them, “Have you submitted, then? Fulfill your vow according to your custom.
For both you and your god have fallen. Allow me, then, to take vengeance on your god.”
But they persisted shamelessly in unbelief and said, “You cannot lay the blame on our god.
For we are the ones at fault, having gone
astray on the road. He has not fallen.” And they put pressure on him
not to carry out what they had promised. So he said to them again, “What do you want, then? Do you believe in my God or in yours?”
They said, “In ours.” And he said to them, “Will you then obey whatever the god falsely so called tells you?”
They all cried out in agreement and gave him their assurance of this. Then the saint, fired up in spirit, ran to the idol.
The idol stood on a high place. He rebuked it and said to it, “I am speaking to you! My Jesus Christ commands you to come down.”

Bowing in fear at the rebuke, the idol fell from its place and rolled toward the saint. It came close to him and stood upright. Everyone was struck with terror, and, astonished at the wonders, they cried out loudly.
He motioned to them with his hand and said, “Have you submitted at least now, or still not at all?”
For they saw someone mocking [?]. Some made a pledge, but others would not submit, saying that this was no great miracle.
But he did not relent toward them. He continued admonishing them and saying, “Oh, how great is your foolishness!
How long will you persist in foolishness? He who is God does not want those
who belong to him and honor him to be like this, but to have such a heart.
Just as he himself is true and good, he commands his own people to be good. Being righteous, he commands his own people to be righteous as well.
And he commands them to be just as he himself, my God, is.
But your god, being stone, has turned your hearts to stone. Being a deceiver and a devil, he wants to deceive you; and being faithless, he has made you faithless too.
Therefore, do not persist in these things, but listen to me and turn away from the worship of demons and from their deception, for they are not gods. Rather, the one I have proclaimed to you is God.
Do you also want to hear from this stone, which you worship, that you are being deceived? Come closer to me and you will hear.
They came closer and watched him intently, hoping to see something greater than what he had already done.
Saint Conon sternly rebuked the idol standing there and said, “Tell me: who is God—you, or the one I proclaim?”
Then, in great fear, the stone god stretched out its hands toward heaven.
It declared in a human voice, saying, “There is one God, there is one Christ, whom you proclaim.”
When this miracle happened, the whole crowd, numbering tens of thousands, cried out in a loud voice, saying, “The one God of Conon has triumphed!”
To this very day, all Isauria and its surrounding regions shout these words as they gather on that glorious day commemorating Saint Conon.
They come out of their homes with candles in the evening and go to the church dedicated to him in the village called Bidana.
As they continued shouting about the glorious miracle, he waved his hand at them and barely managed to quiet them, saying, “At least now acknowledge that you renounce your god.
Allow me, then, to take vengeance on him.” Since many of the people had come to believe, they rushed forward and smashed the idol.

And they were baptized. The rest of them, however, remained disobedient under the devil’s power. Deeply distressed at the destruction of their idol, they devised another plan: to bring the power of a certain evil demon against the holy man.
They had this demon hidden in a cave. It was regarded as a fearsome enemy and destroyer, and they offered it gifts through sacrifices,
not to gain any benefit, but to keep it from harming them. Those who had come to believe begged him to go and drive away that evil
demon. Others were putting him to the test, thinking that he would not be able to overcome it.
But the believers expected Saint Conon to overcome this evil too. He promised them that he would and went with them to the place.
All the people went along, and after lighting candles, they went down into that rocky cleft.
They were very frightened and hesitant. Seeing them hesitate like this, he cried out, saying, “Do not be afraid, for now you will see the outcome.”
He approached the cave in that cleft and commanded the unclean spirit to show itself openly to everyone.
From within, it cried out with pleading words, begging him not to expose its filthy form.
But when he rebuked it, it came out in great fear through an opening, moving along and rolling about. It appeared to everyone like an old woman with torn flesh.
And all the people cried out, shouting the same words as before: “There is one God, the God of Conon! The God of Conon has triumphed!”
And he rebuked that evil-minded demon and forbade it to appear anywhere or harm anyone.
Then Saint Conon sighed over them, saying to them and showing them:
“See who rules over you. See what your gods are.”

[?] They pressed him and led him along with great difficulty. When they were about a stadium away, they considered how to get in to the saint. He remained silent, and looking up, he saw some demons who were afraid of him and held back in fear.
And he ordered them to come to him.
They came and stood before him. He questioned them, saying, “Why have you come?” They said, “What do you command us to do?”
He commanded them with authority, saying, “Do not harm any human being or incite anyone to any evil and filthy deed.”
They said, “These are the things we have been occupied with, and these are the things we delight in: opposing human beings from the beginning. For we have nothing else to do.
So if you wish to release us from these things, command us to do something else, if you wish, and we will do it.
Only do not drive us away in anger to go into deserted places.”
He said to them, “Go to work. Look, those fields opposite are still undug. Go, dig them and clear them.”
When they heard this, they went with great fear to do what they had been commanded.
The robbers came very close to the place and begged their leader, Copius, to approach with them, but they could not persuade him. And leaving
him, they rushed toward the place. Copius, distressed by their plan, remained alone where he was. There he planted his spear, threw down his knife, and sat down.
He rested his head on his knees and wept for them, expecting that nothing good would happen to them.
They approached the saint’s house and knocked on the door. Conon thought they were some of the beggars or sick people who customarily came to him.
He opened the door for them, and when he saw them armed, he thought they had come from a journey to rest.
Each nudged the others, asking where the valuables were kept.
While they searched for valuables, Conon hurried to prepare a meal for them, bringing them wine and urging them to eat. He pleaded with them, saying:
“Come, children, and have something to eat.” But when they did not find what they were looking for, they became angry. They seized him and drew their swords.
They laid their hands on him and tried to force him to bring them his valuables, threatening him and intending to kill him.
There was a great commotion, and the robbers were ready to kill the saint.
Suddenly many demons gathered and came through the efforts of the holy martyr Conon. For they had been commanded that some
should light the ovens in the monastery, while others rushed at the robbers and terrified them,
so that they became as though dead and dropped their swords.

And so, lining them up one at a time and in pairs, they dragged them away. They brought them to the furnace, held their heads against it, and burned them. When they were half dead, they threw them on the ground.
But Saint Conon took pity on them and commanded the demons to leave them, and they left. Seeing that they were exhausted, he prayed for them, and they revived.

When they came to their senses, they rose and fell down before him, repenting of their insolence. They wept, suffering from the pain of their burns, and, lying at his feet, begged him to relieve their great pain.
He prayed, freed them from pain, and sent them away without suffering. When they had been sent away,
they ran off as though driven once again by fire, until they reached the place where Copius, their chief, was.
He looked at them and was astonished to see that they were still alive. Filled with joy, he rose and embraced them because of the most glorious miracle.
When they told him what had happened to them, he rebuked them because they had not listened to him at the beginning.
Then they rose
and went to their homes. They told everyone everything that had happened to them, so that great fear fell upon all who heard.
Even to this very day, fear of Saint Conon remains throughout that region, so that anyone who dishonors his name will soon receive punishment.
So greatly is his name honored because of the grace given to him by the Holy Spirit.
For once there were two wicked men from Saura, who lived in the mountains, terrifying in appearance and with wild hair.
They dishonored his name and disregarded the fear of him. Demons immediately came upon them there, because they had violated the prohibition.
They seized them by the hair and dragged them along. Having bound them, they brought them weeping to the feet of the servant of God.
Fear grew still greater among the unclean spirits, so that, at his command, they cultivated the fields and tended all the gardens and the crops in the fields.
One of these fields was sown with chickpeas. A certain traveler was passing by,
and, thinking it was guarded, saw that the field was good, fruitful, and ripe. Taking a liking to it, he bent down and took as much as he needed.
When he saw that the field was unguarded, he bent down and pulled up the plants
without hesitation. But when he began to bind them into sheaves, he heard a voice saying, “You have enough. Move on.”
He straightened up and looked around but saw no one. He began pulling up the plants again, wanting to make a load for his beast.
The voice kept calling, “You have enough. Do not be greedy.” Again he straightened up but saw no one, and began pulling up the plants just as before.
When he had taken his fill, he tied up the load, intending to put it on his beast. Barely lifting it with great effort, he placed it on his own shoulders.
Immediately the demon that had been calling to him climbed onto the load, so that he could not throw it off.
It sat on his shoulders, beating him, and drove him to the feet of Saint Conon, exhausted and sweating from the weight
and from his wounds. Having brought him to Saint Conon, bound together with the stolen chickpeas, it reviled him, saying:
See, servant of God, that we are not as guilty as disobedient and wicked people.
And now we have done what you commanded: we dug the fields and sowed chickpeas, and they have ripened,
as you yourself can see. But this greedy man came by and, disregarding his fear of you,
picked a great deal with an insatiable heart. I called out to him loudly and repeatedly, saying, “You have enough,
“Man, why are you doing this?” Yet he did not stop, but wronged me too, persisting in his insatiable greed.
And he destroyed our crops, stealing so much all by himself. So what do you say?

When the servant of God saw the man held fast and beaten down by the evils that had befallen him, he took pity on him. First he commanded the unclean spirit to go away and attend to its work, and drove it out.
It went away dejected because the saint had not become angry with the thief.
After rebuking the thief for his greed and instructing him never again to undertake such thefts
or persist in greed, he let him go. This remains in force in those regions to this day: if anyone attempts to steal from the gardens or vineyards,
not only fruit but even leaves, or any kind of seed, on any pretext, it is impossible for him not to be struck down immediately on the spot.
Then, with much prayer and confession, he must bring gold or silver equal in value to what was stolen. Only then will that person be freed from his torment.
The same applies to the birds, which are numerous at the holy tomb,
and to the livestock that people drive there and bring each year for the holy and glorious commemoration: various herds of oxen,
Mares, goats, and sheep in their tens of thousands graze in the mountains without anyone guarding them.
Yet they are guarded by fear, so that no one dares begin to steal or even touch them with impunity. For if the evildoers merely see his name of authority,
or the identifying marks hanging from their necks, they immediately recognize them and keep away.
Thus God honored his life, making him even more glorious after his death.
In addition to these miracles, this also happened. A certain poor widow had an only son who was still nursing. His mother carried him at her breast,
and at harvest time she went to gather ears of grain for her food and laid her son on the ground.
She went over to the reapers and was gathering ears of grain when suddenly a wolf came and found the little child lying there with no one beside him. It seized him and went away.
The reapers heard the infant crying, and his mother heard it and turned around. Realizing the disaster that had befallen her, she cried out along with everyone else.
Some of the reapers shouted, while others ran after the wolf, but they did not catch it and returned.
His mother, without stopping to rest, raised her hands and ran weeping to the holy man to tell him of her misfortune.
When she reached the monastery, the child’s mother cried out loudly, saying, “Saint Conon, give me my son!” Hearing the sound of weeping, he sprang up and went to the door, as was his custom.
When she saw him, she clasped his feet and wept bitterly. He raised her up and asked, “What is the matter?”
Since she was too sorrowful to explain, those who had come with her told him. When he heard what had happened, he took counsel with the child's mother and stood before everyone.
He raised his eyes and hands to heaven and prayed. Calling upon the holy threefold name, he commanded the demons to go and bring back the wolf with the child unharmed.

Having been summoned, they went swiftly and invisibly and caught up with it very far away, still carrying the infant in its mouth. Some seized it by the ears and dragged it, others pushed it from behind, and still others beat it.
Thus they brought the wolf to the feet of Saint Conon. It fell down and laid the child before everyone.
Everyone cried out with a loud voice and, shedding tears of great joy, glorified God for such power given to him.
He took the child from the beast and gave it to its mother. Then, after offering a prayer,
he dismissed everyone, including the wolf. The unclean spirits were also driven out of their idols, and that region began to suffer from smallpox.
But the saint, by the power given to him by the Holy Spirit, drove them out of every part of that region.
He also exposed the others that were harming people. Rebuking the spirits, he summoned and bound them in the name of Jesus Christ.
He put them into thirty jars, secured and bound them, sealed them with lead, and buried them in his house.
This is one of his many miracles of healing, through which his name became renowned and his fame spread. In the account of his life I have mentioned only a few of the many.
A certain governor named Magnus received authority by an imperial command. He was filled with anger against the Christians and said:
“Whoever does not renounce the name of Christ is to be killed.” Filled with anger, he came to the city of Iconium.
In his anger he began to say, “Tell me of anyone you know, here in this city or in other cities, who is a Christian or calls himself one.”
Seeing that he was breathing fury, they informed him fearfully, saying:
“We hear that there is someone named Conon in the mountainous regions who belongs to that faith. They say that great miracles are performed
by him, which astonish us all.” He said, “Tell me where he lives, in a city or a village,
and the name of the city and the village, and how far apart they are.” They said, “The village is called Bidana.
We also hear of another man of that faith, named Nisius, who lives in the village of Usora, along the same road.”
On learning this, he gave orders and hurried to the place. When he reached the village of Usora,
he immediately seized Saint Nisius there and ordered him to be kept under guard. From there he sent men to summon Saint Conon quietly from the village of Bidana on another matter,
so that there would be no disturbance in those places because of him. For he feared those places, having heard that their inhabitants were bold and quarrelsome.

The next morning Magnus took his seat and ordered Saint Nisius to be brought before him, thinking, “Either I will persuade him to renounce the name of Christ, or I will torture him until Saint Conon is brought here.”

When Nisius had been brought in, he began to question him, saying, “What is your name, and what is your station?”—questions of the sort that rulers do not customarily ask everyone. Saint Nisius said, “I am a Christian.”
And he ordered him to be beaten. Saint Nisius endured it for the sake of his good confession of Christ.
For he was gentle and without malice, and plain in speech. For there was no
weaving of elaborate words on his part, for he did not even know how. But he was courageous in faith and endurance. He gave him no other answer, but only, “I am a Christian.”

Magnus, growing still angrier and wishing to overcome him, ordered harsher blows to be inflicted on him, so that he would die under them before Conon arrived. Those who were beating him struck without mercy.
After being beaten and enduring these wounds for many hours, he gave up his soul without a sound.
Thus Saint Nisius nobly and devoutly completed his confession for Christ in his own village of Usora.
The governor Magnus had sought to attain this office for no other reason than to bring destruction upon Christians.
Having sent to Videna to summon Saint Conon by deceit, he remained in the village of Usora for no other reason than to kill the saint together with Nisius, which he indeed did.
Having readied a horse and a man, he quickly sent them to the village of Videna, where Saint Conon was.
And immediately he sat down on the judgment seat and ordered him to be brought in.
All those who had assembled at the governor’s command were distressed when they saw the saint appearing before them. They wept and dared not say anything.
For they saw his gray hair, white as wool, his handsome body, and his smiling eyes,
his face cheerful in old age.
When he was brought before the governor, there was great weeping among those standing there on his account.
The governor, wishing to frighten him, ordered the instruments of torture to be laid before him and began to entice him with words, saying:
“Seeing that you are old and adorned with such gray hair, I believe that you also possess great wisdom. Therefore show understanding worthy of your gray hair, and [?] deception and folly.
“The name of Christ—I do not know where it came from among you—reject and renounce it, and through me you will become a friend of the emperor
“and of all the rulers. From them you will receive every good thing, and whatever pleases you and is precious to you will be yours.
“And, above all, you will be given the priesthood of the great gods,
“as is fitting for no one else, but for your dignity and your marvelous gray hair. I know that you will love me myself, since I will have procured not only these things for you, but many others.
“So if my words and promises please you, raise your head and give your assent. Do not be ashamed. Cast off your nakedness and clothe yourself in purity.
“And do not oppose me as Nisius did.”
The servant of God was unskilled and unpracticed in the Greek language.
But as the grace of the Holy Spirit flowed toward him,
He answered clearly in the Isaurian language, saying, “Did you come hurrying here just for this, wearing yourself out
and those who serve you? Do you not know that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ—neither flattery,
Neither the threat of death, nor fire, nor the sword. But why do I speak of these things?
What you have placed before me—you think you are mocking me greatly, but you yourself will be greatly mocked.
Angered by these words, Magnus ordered him to be tortured for many hours.
Then, having ordered them to ease off, he cried out angrily, saying, “You speak to me with confidence
and act clever with your words, thinking that with such words you will escape punishment. At least now, then, abandon your foolishness and your senseless Christian hope,
and agree to do as I say.” The saint answered and began to speak against Magnus: “You godless man, worse than any wild beast!
How long will you abuse God’s patience and oppose God? Gods falsely
named are what you set up, and they are the work of human hands, made of stone and wood, unable to walk.
And is it these that you [?] against Christ, who created everything, O rebel against God and enemy

of the truth? Like a wolf you have come against his servants and set out to slaughter them. Just as you tortured and killed Saint Nysius, you are eager to get rid of me in the same way. What wrong have we done

You torture me like this and keep on beating me. You try to force me to abandon the living God, promising the emperor's favor, protection before the rulers, gifts of property, and a defiled priesthood.
Is that what you offer me in exchange for God's gifts?
But may your promise come to nothing for you. Even though you have stripped me of my clothing, you cannot strip me of Christ, in whom I am clothed.
For we have Christ and know one God, who can deliver us, his servants, from your hands. So now do whatever you wish to do.”
Hearing this again, the governor became very angry and ordered them to strip him, bind him, and beat him.
Then he considered what other, more savage tortures he could devise to destroy him by them. While he was considering this,
the people of the city of Isauria heard that he was being beaten, that the governor was torturing Saint Conon. A large crowd quickly gathered under arms and went against him.
The governor realized how large the uprising was and that they had come against him
to help Saint Conon. He had already foreseen that this would happen and had prepared a saddled horse.
Finding it ready, he mounted and fled. He reached the city of Iconium and found safety there.
Some of the Isaurians pursued the governor to capture and kill him. Then, failing to overtake him, they turned back.
Many of the people entered the shed where the governor had been torturing Christ’s servant
and found the saint lying alone on the ground, stretched out.
After untying him, the people saw blood dripping from him, drop by drop. They cried out, weeping and grieving.
Each took some of that blood and anointed their bodies with it, believing that they would be sanctified by it.
They went with him to the monastery. They were deeply distressed and took every care to heal his wounds.

Through their devoted care they restored him to health, and each, showing their faith, bowed down and kissed the righteous man's knees. Then they returned to their homes rejoicing. After these hardships and the sufferings he endured for Christ,
having demonstrated his faith, he lived for two years in a good and glorious old age and reached the end of his life.
Those who were there sent word throughout the whole region of the holy man's death,
announcing it. On hearing this, people gathered together, mourning the saint.
They buried him as their own instructor and teacher,
which he had been to them. They laid him in the tomb where his blessed mother and his blessed betrothed wife, who had always remained a virgin, both lay.
After his death, they set aside his house as a church. While digging the foundations in the presence of the bishop who happened to be there at the time,
they dug down to some earthenware jars. They saw that these were very securely bound and had lead seals.
There were thirty of them. They marveled, wondering what this could be. They wanted to move them but could not, because they were heavy.
They thought they were full of gold or something else. They broke one of them and suddenly saw two dark, fierce beings leap out of the jar. These threw everyone standing there to the ground.
The two made the air dark and gloomy, so that all the ropes of the builders' equipment snapped loose on every side, and what he had built collapsed.
They appeared to everyone in the air, crying out and declaring their names. One said, “I am Diomedes.”
The other said, “I am Kouton.” As a result, great fear fell upon that village, and from then on no one dared to be outside their house after sunset, for the demons strangled many people.
They prevented others who wanted to cross from passing over the bridge.
The other earthenware jars remain to this day in the place where they were laid.
But if anyone asks why the demons broke their pledge to him, it was because people too had transgressed his commandment,
which he always proclaimed as he taught everyone: “Do not be insatiable [?] or greedy for possessions.” He knew that these evil spirits were subject to these vices.
For he had shut them up in jars, and they had remained until then in subjection to Saint Conon.
So, because people transgressed his commandments, the demons likewise transgressed.
After these events, they persevered in fasting and prayers for many days and only with difficulty contained [?] the havoc caused by the two escaped demons.
We have mentioned only a few of the many things. No one can recount the healings he performed during his life and after his death, with God bearing witness to them.
For to him, Christ our God, be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
